claims.text: Nanosecond pulsed-laser processing can directly produce ultrafine high-entropy nanoalloys on a carbonaceous support.
The laser-synthesized high-entropy nanoalloys have particle sizes of approximately 1–3 nm.
The resulting high-entropy nanoalloys exhibit a uniform elemental distribution.
Rapid laser synthesis on carbon produces or supplies a defective interfacial buffer layer at the nanoalloy-support interface.
The proposed interfacial buffer layer is rich in oxygen or carbon vacancies.
A defective carbon support stabilizes ultrafine high-entropy nanoalloys produced by laser-induced thermionic-emission reduction.
An oxygen sublattice can function as a buffer layer in a high-entropy material.
The defective interfacial layer restricts atomic diffusion during high-temperature annealing.
The defective interfacial layer accommodates strain.
Restricting atomic mobility inhibits atomic rearrangements that would otherwise cause phase segregation.
Restricting atomic mobility sustains high configurational entropy during thermal exposure.
The defective buffer layer preserves a metastable, homogeneous single-phase solid solution during annealing at approximately 400–800 °C for several hours.
Comparable nanoalloys lacking the defective interfacial layer will undergo greater diffusion, elemental segregation, and phase transformation under the same annealing conditions.
High-temperature structural evolution and short-range clustering can occur in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The proposed stabilization mechanism is most effective specifically for particles in the 1–3 nm size range.
The proposed stabilization mechanism remains effective up to about 800 °C for laboratory-scale annealing durations.
